# Final Project Review and Defence {#sec-final-review}

A reusable IP release should have claims that another engineer can check. The Wally-controlled AXI/DMA accelerator connects the book's foundations, verification, SoC integration and implementation topics in one system. Correct arithmetic is necessary, but it is only one part of the release: transaction ownership, firmware ordering, verification scope and implementation constraints determine whether the IP can be integrated safely.

Use this chapter for a release review, an independent demonstration or the course's individual defence. The detailed course specification and proposed assessment rubric remain in @sec-hsd-coursework; the executable reference is explained in @sec-executable-project. The questions below examine reasoning about the reader's own changes. Running the supplied reference unchanged shows that your environment is ready, and your own design contribution is a separate piece of work.

Use @sec-complete-case to rehearse a complete evidence review. It joins one locked dot-product RTL release to numerical/formal checks, real Wally firmware, FPGA placement/routing and ASIC GDSII, with actual results and physical visuals. Compare the failing original 100 MHz implementations with the later Nexys and ASIC candidates accepted within their declared gates; explain why the changed ECP5 candidate still misses 100 MHz. Its power and frequency estimates retain their block/model boundaries; no complete-SoC physical or energy claim is inherited.

Students without an FPGA can complete the demonstration with the real-Wally RTL platform: show their firmware-controlled accelerator, polling/interrupt completion, result checks and cycle comparison. Present their synthesis/constraint analysis and generated or instructor-provided implementation-report review for P5, together with the remaining board bring-up plan. Use the [alternative evidence map](labs/NO-FPGA.md). Both routes have the same rubric opportunities; programming, physical IO and DDR validation stay unexecuted where no hardware was available.

## Concepts: what has actually been demonstrated?

### Follow one job across the complete system

Begin the review with a concrete operand vector and a successful job. Explain the numerical contract: signed 16-bit operands occupy the low half of 32-bit memory words, the length is between 1 and 256, and the result is a signed 64-bit dot product stored as two little-endian words. Identify the accepted descriptor, the memory ranges it authorizes and the result the independent model predicts.

Then follow the causal sequence. Firmware initializes shared buffers, programs the control registers and requests START. In the reference platform, Wally issues AHB accesses; the adapter turns them into AXI4-Lite control transactions. The IP validates and latches the descriptor before issuing AXI4 DMA requests. The engine fetches operands, computes the result, writes both result words and reports successful completion only after the write responses have been accepted. Firmware observes completion under the stated ordering contract and checks the complete numerical result. The interrupt case adds terminal-event detection, service and acknowledgement.

Annotate a trace with **accepted** transactions; cycles in which VALID alone is high are not transfers. A successful baseline job has `2*N` DMA reads and two DMA result writes; CPU instructions, descriptor accesses and status polling are separate traffic. Identify at least one stall and show that payload and transaction identity remain stable. Explain why a result word appearing in RAM does not yet tell software that the complete result is ready to consume.

The two-word result is not an atomic 64-bit memory update. A fault or reset can leave a partial result. The completion/error protocol is therefore part of the data-validity contract, not just a user-interface convenience. CPU PMP also does not automatically restrict an independent DMA master. Show where the actual DMA access policy is enforced.

### Separate the integration layers

The reference platform deliberately uses disabled caches, shared simulation RAM, a single-outstanding DMA engine and a simplified direct machine-external interrupt route. It executes real Wally RTL and firmware, but it is not the complete production uncore. Explain which assumptions make the experiment interpretable and what would have to change for cached buffers, a PLIC, multiple bus masters or separate clock/reset domains.

| Boundary | Required explanation | Evidence that belongs to this boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Numerical IP | Widths, signedness, parameters, result validity | Independent model, corner vectors and arithmetic comparisons |
| AXI4-Lite control | Independent AW/W, byte strobes, retained responses and active-descriptor protection | Accepted register transactions and control/error checks |
| AXI4 DMA | Address policy, request/response ownership, error termination and completion ordering | DMA trace, conservation checks and adversarial stalls/errors |
| Wally integration | AHB adapter, address map, memory attributes and interrupt service | Firmware, adapter checks and real-core simulation logs |
| Implementation | Technology, constraints, representation and operating corners | Netlist/equivalence, STA or measured board/physical results, as applicable |

An observed PASS at one boundary does not inherit the obligations of the next. A generic synthesis result cannot establish a board clock frequency, and a routed layout cannot establish manufacturing-test coverage.

### Connect the release to RA5–RA8

Use the learning outcomes as an evidence map; four headings that repeat the same screenshots would say little.

| Outcome | Final claim | Evidence to bring to the review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RA5: design from specification to RTL and platform integration | The specified function is implemented and controlled by firmware on the agreed platform | Requirements, architecture, RTL, address map and successful CPU/DMA/interrupt integration |
| RA6: reusable IP architectures and hardware design patterns | Arithmetic, protocol and platform policy have clear reusable boundaries | Interfaces, parameter contracts, supported configurations and a demonstrated reuse/change case |
| RA7: testability, manufacturability, security and reliability | Relevant failure and implementation risks have been analysed within the agreed scope | Reset/error policy, DMA threat model, DFT/physical-view review, constraints and explicitly missing checks |
| RA8: testing, formal verification and IP security evaluation | The submitted configuration has independent checks and completed formal/security evidence with stated limits | Model/tests, negative-control results, formal harness/results, security cases and requirement-to-evidence links |

For each claim, identify the exact configuration and the person who can explain it. If the result is instructor-provided, state that provenance. If a check is not run, retain that status and the reason; an implementation plan can support analysis but cannot replace the missing execution evidence.

## Implementation: assemble a reviewable IP release

### Freeze the release candidate

Choose the Git revision and define which student sources, generated views and external dependencies form the candidate. Record the Wally revision, tool/container identities, compiler flags, firmware ISA/ABI, clocks, memory attributes, address map, parameters and seeds. Identify the reference implementation separately from student variants. Chapter-listing synchronization leaves a student implementation untouched, so never regenerate or overwrite it there.

The release should contain a concise top-level index from requirements to design mechanisms and evidence. File names such as `final.v` or screenshots labelled “passed” are insufficient without configuration and checker provenance. Large waveforms and physical results can be immutable artifacts referenced by hashes and stable locations.

| Release item | Minimum content | Review check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specification | Numerical contract, register map, legal descriptors, reset/error/completion policy | Every externally visible behavior has an acceptance criterion |
| RTL and integration | Module boundaries, sources/parameters, bus adapter and platform connections | The submitted source/configuration is the one that was checked |
| Software/model | Driver/firmware, independent oracle, linker/memory assumptions | The oracle does not repeat the RTL algorithm's same defect |
| Verification | Tests, properties, assumptions, bounds, seeds, logs and counterexamples | Results have a stated scope and fresh source/artifact identities |
| Implementation views | Constraints, netlists and any available physical/board views | Views agree on ports, parameters, clocks and represented technology |
| Risk review | DMA policy, reset/fault behavior, CDC where applicable, DFT and fabrication obligations | Remaining risks are explicit and connected to the release scope |
| Reproduction/origin | Entry commands, environment identities, source licenses and third-party notices | Another engineer can reproduce the promised experiment and identify reused material |

Use @sec-verification-methodology to keep the representation hierarchy consistent. “Verified RTL,” “equivalent netlist,” “timing-closed design,” “physically checked layout” and “tested silicon” describe different milestones. State only the milestones for which the candidate has evidence.

### Explain the hard decisions

Select two or three design choices and compare them with feasible alternatives. Useful examples include a single-outstanding DMA schedule, separate numerical and bus modules, descriptor locking while BUSY, a widened range validator, uncached buffers or the choice of completion acknowledgement. Explain the constraint that made each choice reasonable and the property that would need revisiting if it changed.

For a performance extension, show the cost as well as the benefit. Bursts or multiple outstanding reads change ordering, capacity and error-drain obligations. Caches change software ownership and maintenance requirements. A pipeline register changes latency and potentially the backpressure contract. Reuse is demonstrated by a supported change that keeps the external contract and still passes the relevant checks, and a parameter declaration alone shows less.

Physical and test considerations also belong in the decision record. Explain the timing assumptions attached to the chosen constraints, what state a scan/reset strategy would expose, and which PDK/library/DFT dependencies remain external. If no physical implementation was completed, describe the missing views and checks precisely instead of estimating a fabrication-ready outcome from an RTL simulation.

### Review security and reliability as behavior

The project has concrete assets: program/stack memory, operand buffers, results and control state. Name the actor that can submit a descriptor and the trusted policy that actor cannot change. Demonstrate invalid length, alignment, range wraparound and destination/source overlap rejection before DMA requests are emitted. Explain why testing only individual start/end addresses would miss a range-crossing defect.

Examine one reset or error trace with a transaction already accepted. Describe which state is cleared, which outstanding obligation remains at the platform boundary and which memory effects persist. The reference assumes coordinated reset; extending reset independence requires a reviewed recovery protocol. An error code must prevent software from interpreting a partially written destination as a valid completed result.

Claim protection only against threats you tested. The reference range policy leaves side-channel resistance, authenticated firmware, a protected multi-tenant interconnect and complete system isolation open. Scope a security conclusion to the actual mechanism, actor and evaluated cases.

## Hands-on Experiments: the final demonstration

### Prepare evidence before the defence

Reproduce the agreed candidate in the recorded environment and preserve its outputs. Run the automatic suite and the explicit real-Wally entry as described in @sec-reproducible-labs. Keep the unit report at `labs/build/report.json` and the system report at `labs/build/wally-platform/report.json`; using separate build namespaces prevents the system run from erasing the unit evidence.

The reference collector can check freshness and mapped completion records:

```sh
python labs/verification/evidence.py \
  --unit-report labs/build/report.json \
  --system-report labs/build/wally-platform/report.json \
  --output labs/build/verification-evidence.json
```

Run that command in the documented Python environment from the repository/package root. The collector does not execute the missing experiments. Student variants require a reviewed plan and their own source identities; the reference plan cannot grant a reference correctness claim to modified RTL simply because it has the same module name. Archive the raw reports and their referenced artifacts before a subsequent run overwrites them.

The reference formal checks are bounded checks with stated harnesses and horizons, including a reachable completion witness. Report the actual bound and assumptions. Explain what a safety PASS under that bound leaves open: progress over arbitrary durations, complete coverage and signoff. A failing mutation caught by unchanged checking raises confidence in the checker, though it does not show that every possible defect would be caught.

### Demonstration sequence

Prepare the artifacts in advance so the defence can focus on behavior and decisions, with no time lost downloading tools. Where a live rerun is impractical, present preserved outputs with their source/environment identities and explain the reproduction command.

1. **Identity and scope.** Show the candidate revision, student contribution, environment and selected configuration. Identify unrun obligations before presenting results.
2. **Successful standalone job.** Compare a mixed-sign/extreme vector with the independent model. Explain the two result words and a stalled accepted transaction.
3. **Adversarial job.** Show invalid-descriptor rejection with no DMA traffic, or an injected bus error with the specified terminal state. Explain the checked requirement.
4. **Wally firmware integration.** Demonstrate CPU setup, polling completion and complete result comparison, followed by the interrupt-service/acknowledgement case. Trace the AHB-to-AXI4-Lite boundary and the separate DMA path.
5. **Reusable configuration.** Demonstrate a supported configuration or wrapper change and its relevant regression results. State which properties must be re-established.
6. **Independent checker and formal result.** Explain one deliberately detected defect, one property, its assumptions/bound and a non-vacuity or reachability witness.
7. **Implementation and release review.** Present the actual available views, constraints and measurements. Close with the unresolved risks and the evidence index; an unsupported “ready for silicon” claim would undo the defence.

Agree the demonstration duration with the instructor. This sequence is a review aid, not a replacement for the approved assessment rules or the rubric in @sec-hsd-coursework.

### Measure something that answers a question

Choose representative lengths and datasets and compare software with the accelerator under the same Wally configuration. Define measurement boundaries: whether setup, descriptor programming, DMA, polling/interrupt overhead and result checking are inside or outside the reported interval. Preserve the common input and record cycle/instruction counts where actually measured.

An accelerator can lose on a short vector because setup and bus traffic dominate. A useful report explains that result and identifies the crossover or limiting mechanism. Avoid converting simulation cycles into an achieved board frequency. Report generic synthesis resources separately from device-specific placement/routing or ASIC area/timing results. Follow @sec-architecture-exploration when making a controlled comparison; the illustrative CSV is not a physical Wally measurement.

### Questions for individual defence

Use these questions to select evidence and expose assumptions. Answers should refer to the submitted design, a trace, a property or a measurement, not only a textbook definition.

| Topic | Defence question | Evidence to discuss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Numerical contract | Why are your operand/product/accumulator widths sufficient, including the most negative signed operand? | Independent calculation and extreme-value checks |
| Reuse | Which module could be integrated without AXI, and which supported change demonstrates reuse? | Interface contract and a checked variant |
| Control protocol | What happens when AW and W arrive in different cycles or the response is stalled? | Channel/state trace and unchanged payloads |
| DMA accounting | How do you prove that an accepted operand response is used exactly once? | Acceptance-based scoreboard or conservation property |
| Completion | Why is DONE too early if it follows the last write request rather than the accepted responses? | Result-write trace and early-completion negative control |
| Address policy | How does your validator detect wraparound and a source range crossing the trusted boundary? | Widened arithmetic and rejected descriptor case |
| Integration | Why is Wally's AHB interface not simply renamed AXI, and which adapter limitation matters? | Address/data phases, wait/error handling and supported transfers |
| Memory ownership | What changes if D-cache is enabled for the DMA buffers? | Attributes, ordering, ownership and maintenance plan |
| Interrupts | What clears the source of the interrupt, and how does this reference differ from a PLIC-based system? | Firmware service and acknowledgement trace |
| Reset/error | Which accepted obligations and memory writes survive the failure case you selected? | Reset/error waveform and recovery policy |
| Formal scope | What did the solver establish, under which assumptions and for which horizon? | Harness, command/result, witness and stated limitations |
| Independence | Which defect would pass a checker that merely repeated your RTL, and how did your checker detect it? | Oracle design and unchanged negative-control test |
| Performance | Is the observed benefit due to computation, memory behavior or measurement boundaries? | Common input/configuration and cycle/traffic results |
| Physical/test views | Which check separates your current deliverable from a physically qualified or manufacturable IP? | View inventory, constraints, DFT and missing-check register |
| Release integrity | How would another engineer detect stale evidence after you changed one RTL parameter? | Source/configuration hashes and freshness checks |

Each team member should explain at least one transaction, a reuse decision, a verification/security result and a physical/reliability limitation. A contribution matrix and version history identify work, while the defence establishes understanding.

### Make the release decision explicit

Finish with a requirement-level closure table. Use PASS only when the named check completed successfully for the submitted candidate; use FAIL for a contradiction, NOT RUN/INCOMPLETE for absent or unfinished checks, and N/A only with a reviewed scope justification. Identify illustrative examples, reference evidence and student evidence separately.

A release decision should state the intended consumer and supported boundary. For example, a simulation-qualified uncached single-clock accelerator can be useful and reusable while still needing clock-domain analysis, physical timing/DFT views or cached-system integration. Those obligations define the next engineering step. Keep them visible, because a green CI badge hides them.

The final achievement is the ability to connect a specification to RTL, observe its behavior in a real processor platform, challenge the implementation with independent checks and explain the limits of the resulting IP package. That evidence is what makes the design transferable to another engineer and provides a defensible starting point for further implementation.

## Key ideas {#review-summary-ideas .unnumbered .unlisted}

- A reusable release states what was demonstrated and what remains unresolved.
- Defence connects each design decision to requirements, evidence and limitations.

## What you should now be able to explain {#review-summary-explain .unnumbered .unlisted}

Explain one complete project job and justify the claims supported by your own implementation and reports.

## Common mistakes {#review-summary-mistakes .unnumbered .unlisted}

Unit, system and physical results answer different questions, so reporting them as one undifferentiated PASS loses information. A successful reference run is also no reason to leave missing evidence unmentioned; list it as unfinished work.

## Try it yourself {#review-summary-try .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Core · P5 · C0](learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-summary-review .learning-activity}

Rehearse the existing demonstration with one allowed job and one rejected request. Trace each claim back to its recorded source/configuration.
